titre: A Body of Law You Could Finally Hold in One Hand
accroche: Before 1804, France applied hundreds of different customs. The Civil Code fits in a single volume, and reads without Latin.
contenu_vulgarise:
Before the Revolution, there was no such thing as French law in the singular. The north of the kingdom lived under customs, written or not, that varied from one province to the next and sometimes from one town to its neighbor. The south applied a written law inherited from Roman law. On top of these came royal ordinances, canon law, local usages, and the case law of the parlements, the kingdom's high courts. Knowing which rule applied to a marriage, an inheritance, or a sale meant first knowing where you were, and knowing a body of material that no private individual could own.

## What a Single Volume Changes

The *Code civil des Français* (Civil Code of the French) is promulgated on March 21, 1804. It replaces this pile of rules with a single text, applied in the same way across the whole territory.

Two traits matter as much as its content. It is written in everyday French, not Latin, in a deliberately spare language: short articles, simple sentences, very few cross-references. And it is organized systematically, in books dealing with persons, with property, and then with the ways of acquiring ownership. You can look up an answer in it without being a lawyer.

The Code also lays down rules about its own operation, which seem technical and are political. A law applies only after it has been promulgated and published. It does not provide for the past. The judge may not lay down a general rule through his decisions, but he also may not refuse to judge on the grounds that the law is obscure. In other words, the law can be known in advance, and the judge applies it rather than making it.

Napoleon did not draft the text, but he chaired many sessions of the Council of State (Conseil d'État), where the draft was debated, and personally pushed to overcome resistance.

## Why It Traveled So Far

The Code was applied in the territories France controlled, then kept or imitated long after France left. It inspired civil codes in many countries, from Romania to Mauritius, and Louisiana still bears its mark.

This influence was not due to armies alone. It was also due to what a code offered the states then being built: a complete, coherent civil law, available immediately, which they could simply adopt instead of producing it by sedimentation over centuries.

That is where the shift lies. People remember the Code for its content, often to criticize some of its provisions, notably on the position it gave women. But what was truly exported was a form: the idea that law can be written all at once, in order, published, and readable by those it applies to. It is this form, more than its articles, that went around the world.

repere.texte: The Civil Code of the French is promulgated on March 21, 1804. It replaces the customs of the north and the written law of Roman origin in the south with a single text, written in French and not in Latin.
repere.source: Code civil des Français (Civil Code of the French), promulgated on 30 Ventôse, Year XII (March 21, 1804)

carte.punch: What went around the world was not its content. It was its form.
carte.idee: Before 1804, France applied different customs in the north and Roman law in the south, and no one could own that body of material. The Civil Code replaces it with a single volume, in everyday French, organized to be consulted. It is this form that other countries adopted.

quiz.question: According to the entry, what best explains the spread of the Civil Code outside France?
choix: Military force, as occupied territories kept the text after the armies left
The recognized superiority of its provisions on the family and on property
A treaty obligation for France's allies to adopt it
The form of the code itself, a complete and orderly body of law that a state could adopt instead of building it over centuries
quiz.explication: The Code was imposed in the territories France controlled, but above all it was kept and imitated afterward. It offered states under construction a coherent, published civil law available immediately: it is this form, more than the detail of its articles, that was exported.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Before 1804, what did the south of the kingdom apply in civil law?
choix: A written law inherited from Roman law
Exclusively oral customs, with no written trace at all
Canon law, the only law in force across the whole territory
Royal ordinances, the only rules applicable in the south of the kingdom
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The south of the kingdom applied a written law inherited from Roman law, distinct from the customs that governed the north, themselves written or not depending on the province.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the Civil Code of 1804 say about the judge's role when facing an obscure law?
choix: The judge must send the case back to the legislator to clarify the law
The judge may not refuse to judge on the grounds that the law is obscure
The judge may suspend judgment until the text is reformed
The judge applies local custom in the absence of a clear law
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Code provides that the judge may not lay down a general rule through his decisions, but also may not refuse to judge by pleading that the law is obscure: he must decide.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How is the Civil Code of 1804 organized?
choix: In alphabetical order of legal concepts
In a single book, with no internal subdivision
In books dealing with persons, with property, and then with the ways of acquiring ownership
In articles sorted by the province where they apply
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Code is organized systematically, in books devoted to persons, to property, and then to the ways of acquiring ownership, which makes it possible to look up an answer without being a lawyer.
